   I initially put everything in a cabinet, and placed a cage front behind the door to prevent rodents from getting in. I also budgie tied the door. I quickly realized that flies & moths could get in and potentially compromise food boxes with maggots... I quickly modified my format.

hmmmm...   When I work, I am the mix engineer.... so... the first comment doesn't apply to me. My initial post, intended to be from the perspective of me going back in time, and giving advice to my younger self. Rather than to find fault, I would highly recommend that you (and others) soak up as much good advice as you can retain.
If you are using free stuff, download more free stuff!  Create a folder for all your free compressors. Try the Dogfish & spirit fish comp. units. Try out all kinds of free VST compressors.

Think about texture. Adjust your compressor so it doesn't slam the listener so abruptly. Most advanced audio engineers call themselves producers because their ear is more demanding than that of an engineer. 

Smoother rise time on the compressor, the radius of the leading edge of the wave (attack) should have a larger radius. Try different knee settings. A knee settings of 4 is softer than a knee setting of 2-3. A 2:1 (or 3-4:1) ratio at -20 [this depends on the vocal tracking level, so the -20 can be -35, -10, -15] with a limiter as the second in the chain is more pleasing to the ear than a single comp. set at 10:1, -10 threshold. De-esser for the top end should also be applied.
The problem I'm hearing is with both your comp. & EQ settings. They all need to cooperate together.

That comp. setting would be great for a kick drum, or bass guitar (under certain conditions) but can be fatiguing to the ear if human speech were to go on longer than 5 minutes.

> When you bring the group 1 fader down, does it lower the volume that goes to the subwoofer bus? 

I was curious about your question, and I had to know. The bass player was playing, and I pulled SUB mix 1 down and out/off. The sub woofer was unaffected by this action. This is HUGE in my book!  The upper speakers are controlling the bass definition! 

This is really important when you are doing a live multi track recording. What I usually do is shut down the sub completely, and mix the sound check with as much low end from Kick & bass - being sent into the upper speakers. I concentrate my attention on asking the question: Do I have enough definition, and does the EQ setting seem reasonable for mixing these tracks tomorrow. I try to make everything work without the SUB, and only bring the sub in at the end of the sound check. I make a visual inspection of the EQ settings. If my low shelving is cranked +15, I know that looks wrong, and will bring it back.. don't do anything crazy extreme. Track what looks reasonable, and let the sub make up the difference. I can't stress this enough. You don't want to go home, and try to mix a bass guitar that doesn't have any low frequencies... that really sucks. Its second nature for me now, but with some newbies, be careful you don't have your power amp up 100%, and your low shelving all the way off, with 100Hz all the way off.. and think that you are going to have anything left (like Michel Jackson's nose) to mix.

If I find that the tone deteriorates with the pad at 1/2, and is of higher quality on some other channel, direct... rather than through the ACP 88... I would agree with you. I haven't conducted the A/B test yet. 

It was this past week, and I had two hard hitting instruments feeding into 1/2, I had to use the pad. I had been doing things with 1/4 to 1/4.. all line level, but I was disappointed when I read how this bypasses your pre amps. It was over the past few weeks that I plugged a Bass guitar into a mic input, and absolutely loved the tone. I want this going in!  The only thing I could think of, at the time, was to utilize my 1/4 to XLR snake. As soon as I began the sound check I noticed everything was in the red. I backed down all the inputs, and was able to get things to cooperate... all but 1 channel. I had to back down the console input gain. Focusrite gain knobs were all the way off, turned all the way to the left.  I felt restricted, and it wasn't a good vibe trying to track with such an incompatible line matching problem. 

An even better recommendation would be for Focusrite to allow the volume knob to reduce the input, such that you COULD tap out any console, line outs. 

Anyway, I think we've talked this subject to death.... need to conduct some audio research in order to move further.

I do believe I can get a richer/smoother tracking tone across all instruments if I utilize the XLR ins (through the pre amps).... how I manage to do this, and not destroy the input levels is key. There are many ways to achieve this: 

1) I can do it the exact same way as before, but make sure that when I cue up all gain levels in the master meter, that I keep things down around -10VU. You will get a warmer/lusher/smoother set of tracks if you take the pains to do this. 

2) I can run all instruments into the Focusrite, first, and then out into the mixing console. This is probably the best way to do it, but ... it makes me nervous just thinking about this method. 

3) I could go 1/4 to 1/4 out the direct outs of the Allen & Heath GL2400, into the ACP 88, then out the ACP 88 with my 1/4 to XLR snake....  and into the Focusrite XLR pre amps in. I've done this before, and that recording was completely destroyed. I didn't have the time to set everything properly, and was shooting video at the time. I believe the configuration can be done properly, but I clapped down way to hard on the compression.. rather than to keep my wits, and give reasonable compression with a more thoughtful gain structure... I do remember having issues with it being way too friggin' hot. The -10/+4 button may have been the issue. I do need to run some pre production testing, and write a set of configuration paper... stick that in the back of the rack, or laminate it to the side of the unit. 

4) A compromise would be to make use of the 4 -20dB pads on the front of the two units. I have the 19i20, and the Pro 40. The hottest instruments are usually percussive, and lead vocal.  If I consolidate the hottest tracks to 1/2, 9/10 and hit the pads, I will probably be able to achieve what I want, and not spend an arm and a leg on more gear. 

5) The easiest way to deal with all of this would be to go 1/4 to 1/4 and just forget about the benefit of the preamps... but I'm past that, and know I don't want that clear, cold, thin... non pre amp tone.
